newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House banking panel sees fast bank reform law.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House banking panel sees fast bank reform law.

text.p: The U.S. House Banking Committee has set an ambitious schedule for considering legislation to overhaul the U.S. financial services sector, aiming to get a consensus bill to the House floor before the July 4 recess, chairman Jim Leach said Thursday.

With two bills already introduced and two more likely to be introduced, the Iowa Republican said hearings would be held in February and March by the Financial Institutions Subcommittee and the Capital Markets Subcommitee.
After the hearings, a single bill would be introduced for consideration by the full committee in April or May, he said.

Leach's bill would tear down the Glass Steagall Act of 1933 -- allowing one company to offer banking, securities and insurance services. The Federal Reserve would be the primary regulator of integrated financial service companies under the Leach approach.
The bill introduced by New Jersey Republican Rep Roukema would go further and also allow financial services companies to derive up to a quarter of their revenue from non-financial activities.
The Clinton Administration is expected to offer its own proposal in the next few months.

A Treasury Department task force recommended removing all barriers between financial and non-financial companies, people familiar with the task force have said. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin is said to be weighing the recommendations, which have drawn fire from small banks, consumer groups and Leach.

Louisiana Republican Rep. Richard Baker is also preparing legislation. His bill, expected to be identical to a measure Senate Banking chairman Alfonse D'Amato plans to put forth, will likely endorse the approach of mixing financial and non-financial companies.
